questions.behavior: Explain the core benefits of specs: controlling large changes with small edits, reducing context decay, and improving intent fidelity
questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of Spec-Driven Development (SDD) compared to "vibe coding" with AI agents?

options.label: SDD lets the agent work fully autonomously without any human review or intermediate checkpoints, which removes communication overhead and speeds up every part of development.
SDD uses persistent specs to anchor intent across sessions, avoiding the drift that comes from long prompt dialogues.
SDD eliminates the need for version control since specifications replace git history.
SDD requires you to write all the code manually and only use the agent for small suggestions.

questions.behavior: Recognize the human's role as architect and supervisor who supplies context
questions.prompt: In the SDD workflow, how is the developer's role best described?

options.label: A typist who carefully writes most of the production code by hand, only occasionally asking the agent for suggestions on tricky sections, boilerplate, or unfamiliar APIs.
An architect and reviewer who provides the spec and steers the agent, which handles most of the implementation.
A project manager who only creates tickets and never touches code or specs.
A QA tester whose only job is to find bugs in the agent's output.

questions.behavior: Identify the three constitution pillars: mission, tech stack, and roadmap
questions.prompt: In the SDD workflow, what three documents make up a project's "constitution"?

options.label: mission.md, tech-stack.md, and roadmap.md
README.md, CHANGELOG.md, and LICENSE.md
requirements.md, plan.md, and validation.md
user-stories.md, acceptance-criteria.md, and sprint-backlog.md

questions.behavior: Plan a feature spec covering plan, requirements, and validation before coding
questions.prompt: When creating a feature spec in SDD, which three documents are typically written?

options.label: design.md, code.md, and tests.md
plan.md, requirements.md, and validation.md
README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and CHANGELOG.md
mission.md, tech-stack.md, and roadmap.md

questions.behavior: Implement features in small, manageable steps with cleanly cleared context
questions.prompt: What are the three main phases of the SDD feature cycle?

options.label: Research, Write, Deploy
Specify, Compile, Test
Plan, Implement, Validate
Design, Code, Ship

questions.behavior: Keep specs and code in sync to prevent drift and reduce cognitive and AI fatigue
questions.prompt: Why should you ask the agent to make code changes for you instead of editing files directly whenever possible?

options.label: To save context tokens in the agent's memory.
Because developers shouldn't be allowed to touch code in an SDD project.
To prevent drift — the agent can update the related specs at the same time, keeping docs and code in sync.
Because manually editing code is always slower than asking an agent, especially on larger refactors that span multiple files and directories in a project.

questions.behavior: Decide when to handle a change during replanning versus scheduling it as a new roadmap feature
questions.prompt: Why is it important to "replan" between features in the SDD workflow?

options.label: Replanning is only needed when something has gone badly wrong and you need to throw out most of your existing progress and restart the project from scratch.
Replanning is optional and most teams skip it to ship faster.
It's a chance to reflect, update the constitution and roadmap, and refine your workflow — a normal step, not a sign of failure.
Replanning means throwing out your existing constitution and writing a new one from scratch.

questions.behavior: Introduce SDD to brownfield/legacy projects by reverse-engineering specs from existing artifacts
questions.prompt: Can Spec-Driven Development be applied to an existing (legacy) codebase, or only to new projects?

options.label: SDD can only be used on projects that were originally started with an AI agent.
Both. On a legacy project, the agent reverse-engineers a constitution from the existing code and docs, and you continue with the normal workflow.
SDD only works for small personal projects, not production codebases.
SDD is only meant for greenfield projects — any legacy codebase would need a complete rewrite before the workflow could meaningfully be applied to it.

questions.behavior: Apply agent standards such as AGENTS.md, Agent Skills, and ACP to stay agent-independent
questions.prompt: Why is it valuable for an SDD workflow to be "agent-agnostic"?

options.label: The agent landscape moves fast. Keeping specs and tools independent of any single agent lets you switch tools without rebuilding your workflow.
Agent-agnostic workflows are required by law for any enterprise software project.
Agent-agnostic workflows run measurably faster because they avoid vendor-specific optimizations that would otherwise tie your pipeline to a single proprietary runtime.
Agent-agnostic workflows mean you never need to use a coding agent at all.

questions.behavior: Use agent skills to automate repeatable SDD workflows
questions.prompt: What is a "skill" in the context of agentic coding, and when would you create one?

options.label: A skill is a paid plugin you buy from an app store.
A skill is a type of spec that replaces plan.md, requirements.md, and validation.md.
A reusable package of instructions and resources that gives an agent a repeatable capability — handy when you catch yourself retyping the same prompts.
A skill is a special kind of AI model that only certain commercial agents support, usually offered as a paid upgrade on top of the base model you started with.
